---
applyTo: "spec/models/**/*.rb"
---

# Model specs

- In model specs, build the record under test with `described_class.new` and only the attributes the example needs, e.g. `described_class.new(status: :published)` in `spec/models/post_spec.rb`. You MUST NOT use a factory for it.
- In model specs, name the `subject` after the model and use `is_expected` where possible, e.g. `subject(:post) { described_class.new }`. When an example needs a record with different attributes, build it in the example, e.g. `post = described_class.new(title: "A title")`, instead of adding a `let` or another `subject`.
- In model specs, group examples in a `describe` block named after the method, e.g. `describe "#published?"`. For an association, name the block after the association and put the examples for its id attribute in it too, e.g. `author_id` examples in `describe "#author"`.
- In model specs, give each gem's modules heading one `describe` block named after the gem, holding everything under that heading: what the gem's setup does and the methods of its `concerning` block, e.g. `describe "FriendlyId"` containing `describe "#slug"` and `describe "#should_generate_new_friendly_id?"`. You MUST NOT add a `describe` block for that `concerning` block.
- In model specs, give each `concerning` block under `### Public Methods ###` one `describe` block named after it, holding all its methods, including scopes and class methods, e.g. `describe "Publishing"` containing `describe "#recently_published?"`. Keep it in the model's spec, not in a separate file.
- In model specs, order `describe` blocks in four tiers, each in alphabetical order: class methods and scopes, then instance methods, attributes and associations, then modules, then concerns, e.g. `describe ".recent"`, then `describe "#author"` and `describe "#published?"`, then `describe "FriendlyId"`, then `describe "Publishing"`.
- In model specs, test an attribute that uses a custom validator with the validator's matcher, e.g. `it { is_expected.to validate_isbn_format_of(:isbn) }`. You MUST NOT repeat the cases from the validator's own spec.
- In scope specs, create the records with factories and check the records the scope returns, e.g. `create(:post, created_at: 2.days.ago)` and `expect(described_class.recent).to eq([newer_post, older_post])`. Prefer this to comparing `to_sql`.
- Test a callback by what it does, through the call that triggers it, in the `describe` block of the attribute it changes. Say the trigger in the description, e.g. `it "is set when a published post is saved"` in `describe "#published_at"`. You MUST NOT call the callback method directly or test that the callback is registered. When the callback has a condition, test both sides of it.
- Test a save callback by building the record with a factory and calling `save!`, e.g. `build(:post, status: :published, published_at: nil)` then `post.save!`. Test a validation callback by calling `validate` on a record built with `described_class.new`, e.g. `it "is set from the body when validated"` with `described_class.new(body: "word " * 400)` then `post.validate`.
- Test a normalisation in its attribute's `describe` block by building the record with the untidy value and reading it back, e.g. `it "is stripped"` with `expect(described_class.new(title: "  A title  ").title).to eq("A title")`. You MUST NOT call `validate` or `save` for it.
- In model specs, test each `UserAccess` role with `grant_user_access`, which checks `user_is_<role>?` and `for_user_as_<role>` together, e.g. `expect(post).to grant_user_access(user, as: :coauthor)`. Check that a role is withheld with `not_to`, e.g. `expect(post).not_to grant_user_access(user, as: :coauthor)`. Pass a record, an array or a relation, e.g. `expect(drafts).to grant_user_access(user, as: :copy_editor)`. Create the records with factories.
- Put the `grant_user_access` examples straight in `describe "UserAccess"`, in role rank order. You MUST NOT group them in a `describe` for a role or a method, e.g. `describe "copy editor"`. Give any other method in the block its own `describe` as usual. Name each after what it grants or denies, and to whom, e.g. `it "grants drafts to a copy editor"`. For each role, write an example that grants it and one that denies it to a user without the role. When the role has a condition, test a record on each side of it, e.g. `it "denies a published post to a copy editor"`.
